title: Long context + high TPS stress walkthrough - Redwood demo
summary: Redwood AE/SE walk through an edge-case focused demo simulating long conversation contexts, high TPS, and streaming backpressure. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a real-time analytics assistant. Key asks: tail-latency under load, graceful streaming reconnects, quantization/kv cache effects on long context, and SLA pricing for bursty traffic.
topics: long context handling and KV/prefix caching
high TPS stress and autoscaling behavior
action_items: Alice - send synthetic benchmark script and results spreadsheet by 2026-11-18
Ben - capture debug logs from the demo run and share zip
Mike - share expected peak TPS patterns and SLOs (by 2026-11-17)
next_steps: Redwood to circulate stress-test harness and pricing tiers for dedicated bursts
Schedule follow-up POC scoping call for week of 2026-11-22
Customer to confirm compliance docs needed for procurement
transcript:
[00:00] Alice Nguyen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we've got about 70 minutes blocked. We'll run through the edge-cases demo focusing on very long conversation contexts, a high TPS synthetic workload, and streaming behaviors when the system gets backpressured. Ben and I will tag-team. 

[00:18] Mike Patel: Sounds good. Quick context from us: Parity is building an internal analyst assistant that keeps an entire quarterly data dump in context. Peak bursts happen at the start of market hours — roughly 1k TPS for short windows, and sustained lower levels later. We're evaluating if hosted Redwood is okay or we need Dedicated.

[00:35] Ben Carter: Great, thanks Mike. Real quick on participants: Ben, SE; Alice, AE; Mike and team on the call. I'll kick off with the runtime behavior for long contexts and then we'll fire the harness. 

[00:50] Sara Gomez: One ask up front — how tolerant is the streaming API to partial reconnects? Our front end will attempt to reconnect and glue partial chunks together.

[01:05] Ben Carter: Good question. We have two behaviors: streaming with resumable sequences using prefix KV cache, and stream-with-restart which yields partial outputs then restarts generation. The resumable path keeps the KV cache per-session so we can avoid re-computing earlier tokens. We'll demo both. Note: resumable requires a session ID and we're going to show the Console trace.

[01:28] Jordan Lee: Are there quantization or 4-bit artifacts we should watch for with very long contexts? We've seen hallucinations when context is near model max.

[01:40] Alice Nguyen: Short answer: quality is a function of model variant and quantization profile. Our Optimize tool flags tokens with higher perplexity drift when KV cache or quantization interacts badly. Ben will show the dashboard.

[01:52] Ben Carter: Okay, jumping in. I'm sharing my screen — Console -> Sessions -> Demo-Stress -> Live Trace. You can see three streams: control plane events, token stream, and metrics (per-stream latency).

[02:08] [Ben shares screen briefly, some chatter] 

[02:22] Ben Carter: First scenario: long context walk-through. We're using a 250k token synthetic context split into prefix chunks. We pinned a Redwood-verified open model 'rwd-large-v1' quantized to int8 for the run. This simulates your quarter dump. Observe the KV cache warm-up phase — large memory footprint but subsequent requests hit the cache. 

[02:45] Mike Patel: 250k? Our actual is closer to 180k, so this is a good upper bound. Are you chunking context server-side or expecting us to pre-chunk?

[02:58] Ben Carter: Server-side chunking is supported. We do automatic prefix shingling and maintain chunk indexes in the session so you can submit whole objects. For Dedicated you can opt to increase cache retention TTLs.

[03:14] Sara Gomez: How do cache TTLs interact with autoscaling? If a node is evicted, do we lose warm cache?

[03:22] Ben Carter: On Hosted, we try to keep session affinity for active workloads, but eviction can happen. We persist the prefix index to fast storage and reconstruct KV cache on new node attach — there's a warm-up cost. On Dedicated with pinned GPU pools, you can get higher retention and pinned memory which reduces warm-up. 

[03:40] Jordan Lee: What about tail latency numbers? We care about P95 and P99 when the cache is cold vs warm.

[03:47] Ben Carter: Good metric. For this model on this GPU class: cold P95 is ~420ms per token generation step, cold P99 jumps to 1.2s for certain long sequences. Warm cache reduces P95 to ~120ms and P99 to ~260ms. We'll show those numbers as we run.

[04:05] Alice Nguyen: Quick note — these are synthetic numbers and will vary by sequence length and prompt shape. For your workload we'll run the harness with your token length distribution. 

[04:18] Ben Carter: Alright I'm launching the long-context single-session flow. You should see CPU/GPU charts spike and the KV hit-rate increase after a few requests. 

[04:35] [sound of typing; slight network glitch] 

[04:50] Alice Nguyen: There's a little hiccup on my end — looks like the console lost reconnect to telemetry for a second.

[04:56] Ben Carter: That's fine, reconnect's normal. The session keeps producing tokens. You can see streaming tokens arriving in the UI. Notice the 'inflight tokens' metric. 

[05:10] Mike Patel: I'm seeing tokens but occasionally there's a chunk gap — tokens 1200-1210 missing then stream resumes with token 1211. Is that likely a transcript artifact?

[05:25] Ben Carter: Could be a packet drop or the streaming client decided to coalesce chunks. There's a configurable 'chunk_size' param; smaller chunks reduce perceived gap but increase overhead. We recommend 128 token chunks for UI streaming.

[05:40] Sara Gomez: If we get a partial chunk and attempt to reconnect, how do you guarantee idempotence? We can't allow duplicate actions.

[05:48] Ben Carter: Each chunk carries a monotonically increasing seq number and a session checksum. The client can request replays from the last acked seq. For exactly-once semantics to downstream side-effects, the app needs to de-dupe on server-assigned request IDs.

[06:05] Jordan Lee: Now the second scenario: high TPS stress. We're going to simulate many short requests concurrently. Do you want us to kick the harness?

[06:12] Ben Carter: Go ahead — launching the TPS generator to target sustained 800 TPS with bursts to 1.2k. On the right you can watch autoscaler decisions.

[06:24] [burst of console logs, simulated requests, fan noise audible] 

[06:40] Ben Carter: Autoscaler sees CPU/GPU queues cross threshold and provisions additional instances. For Hosted we have ephemeral burst pools that we route to. For Dedicated you can pre-book burst capacity or configure overflow to Hosted.

[06:57] Mike Patel: What's the expected warmup when autoscaling? We can't accept big latency spikes at market open.

[07:04] Ben Carter: Usually node boot and model load takes ~30-60s depending on model size. We mitigate with predictive pre-warming if your schedule is known. Also we can use a warm standby with a lightweight model variant that responds fast for short time windows.

[07:20] Sara Gomez: Is that the 'fallback policy' you mentioned? Where you fallback to a smaller model to keep latency low?

[07:27] Ben Carter: Exactly. You can set policy rules — e.g., if queue latency exceeds X, route to rwd-medium-v1 with same prompt templates. It's exposed in the Console under Routing -> Fallbacks.

[07:40] Jordan Lee: While the TPS generator is running, can you show what happens to streaming backpressure?

[07:45] Ben Carter: Sure. I'm toggling an artificial network delay on one of the nodes to simulate slow sinks. Watch the per-stream backpressure metric. 

[07:58] [UI shows per-stream latency graph climbing] 

[08:05] Ben Carter: When backpressure occurs, we apply two levers: adaptive batching throttling and progressive chunking. Adaptive batching reduces batch sizes for slow nodes, and progressive chunking increases chunk granularity to avoid head-of-line blocking. You can see throttles applied here.

[08:24] Mike Patel: Do you drop requests or queue them? We can't queue indefinitely.

[08:30] Ben Carter: There's a configurable max-queue-per-worker. Once that's hit, the router can either reject with 503, enqueue to overflow, or route to fallback. For a real-time assistant we usually prefer fallback to a smaller model or to degrade to cached answers.

[08:45] Karen Wu: From procurement: what's the SLA for dropped requests in Hosted? We need numbers for procurement.

[08:52] Alice Nguyen: Hosted has a best-effort SLA; Dedicated has explicit SLOs you can buy with credits for burst capacity and a guaranteed failover path. We'll include SLA matrices in the follow-up email.

[09:05] Ben Carter: Back to the demo — you can see error spikes in the logs around the burst peak. I'm pulling a sample log to show the router decision tree. See this entry: 'route: fallback -> rwd-medium-v1 due to queue_latency > 200ms'.

[09:25] Sara Gomez: Can we bias routing by customer tier so high-priority users always get Dedicated capacity and others hit Hosted?

[09:31] Ben Carter: Yes — routing policies can be tokenized by API key, route, or customer attribute. You can map priority fields to routing rules. 

[09:44] Jordan Lee: Are there costs for constant fallback to Hosted from Dedicated? That dynamic billing concerns us.

[09:51] Alice Nguyen: Billing is metered per-route. We'll graph costs for typical fallback ratios in the pricing sheet. For budgeting it's often recommended to set a cost cap and alerting.

[10:05] Mike Patel: Let's test an induced timeout now. We want to see state cleanup, client behavior, and how partial outputs are surfaced.

[10:12] Ben Carter: I'm hard-killing one of the worker processes to simulate a mid-generation timeout. Watch the session state. 

[10:25] [audible intake of breath] 

[10:28] Ben Carter: Worker died. Router is failing over the session. Console shows session marked degraded and a partial output sent upstream. There's an auto-retry configured here: 2 attempts with exponential backoff. It tried a retry to a warm fallback node and resumed token generation at seq+1.

[10:50] Sara Gomez: In that case did we lose KV cache? The resumed session looks to have a small quality drop.

[10:58] Ben Carter: There was a KV reconstruction step; some early attention state wasn't fully recovered, which showed as a slight semantic drift. For mission-critical flows we recommend sticky nodes or Dedicated with persistent backing to avoid that.

[11:12] Jordan Lee: Any way to snapshot KV to persistent store frequently? We could accept extra write overhead.

[11:18] Ben Carter: Yes — you can set KV checkpoint cadence. It trades latency for resilience. We'll include recommended settings in the benchmark notes.

[11:30] Mike Patel: Let's talk about Optimize recommendations — you've mentioned intelligent batching and quantization. Show us how Optimize suggests changes based on observed metrics.

[11:38] Ben Carter: Switching to the Optimize tab. You see a heatmap of tokens-per-request vs latency vs cost. For your observed throughput, Optimize suggests moving to per-route batching with max_batch=64 and enabling int4 quantization for rwd-medium-v1 during off-peak hours. It also suggests increasing prefix cache TTL to 6 hours for certain routes.

[11:58] Alice Nguyen: Note that quantization savings are model and prompt dependent. We'll help run A/B tests. Optimize ties to eval sets so you can monitor quality regressions automatically.

[12:10] Jordan Lee: Can Optimize generate automated rollout plans — like canary to 10% then 50% then full with failback?

[12:17] Ben Carter: Yes. The Rollouts page supports canary percentages, time windows, and automatic regression-based rollback. You can configure per-metric thresholds and hold durations.

[12:30] Mike Patel: Back to streaming — what's your recommendation for front-end reconnection UX? Should we stitch partial responses or show a 'reconnecting' placeholder?

[12:38] Alice Nguyen: Many teams show partial text and a 'loading' indicator. Stitching works but ensure dedupe against seq numbers. For critical results, we also recommend a confidence/freshness marker when resumed after failure.

[12:55] Sara Gomez: We've seen a pretty bad user experience when the model restarts and repeats earlier info. Any guardrails?

[13:03] Ben Carter: Use last-ack seq and have the client send a delta prompt that says 'continue from token N' rather than full context resend. Also use server-side de-duplication and a short overlap window to avoid repeated sentences.

[13:20] Karen Wu: From procurement: do you have references of customers who ran similar high-burst workloads and stayed on Hosted?

[13:28] Alice Nguyen: Yes, we'll anonymize a couple of case studies. Short answer: some customers stayed hosted using predictive pre-warming and fallbacks; others moved to Dedicated for guaranteed performance. We'll share the playbooks.

[13:45] Ben Carter: Now spinning up the mixed-workload test: long-context sessions kept alive while short queries hammer throughput. This stresses prefix retention and routing.

[13:58] [console log stream intensifies] 

[14:12] Ben Carter: Interesting — a few long sessions got evicted due to memory pressure; the router attempted reconstruction and issued partial outputs. See log 'kv-evict: session 0x8f3 -> reconstruct attempt 1'.

[14:30] Mike Patel: Eviction is our nightmare. Can Dedicated be configured to reserve X GB per session?

[14:37] Ben Carter: Yes, with Dedicated you can reserve session memory pools and pin important sessions, but it's a tradeoff against concurrency. We'll help you model cost vs concurrency for session-pinning.

[14:50] Jordan Lee: Do you have tooling to simulate our exact distribution so we can understand eviction risk?

[14:55] Ben Carter: We do — the stress harness can take a histogram of session lengths and peak concurrency and run Monte Carlo sims. Alice will send the harness and a short README.

[15:10] Mike Patel: Can you show logs for a session that was partially served then fell back to rwd-small for 30s? We want to see how clients are notified.

[15:18] Ben Carter: Showing sample trace: 'session 0x9a2 route->fallback rwd-small reason=queue_latency'. The stream emits an 'engine_change' frame to clients with metadata about model, reason, and seq. Clients can decide how to render this.

[15:40] Sara Gomez: What about security — will routing metadata ever leak user PII?

[15:46] Ben Carter: Routing metadata is control-plane only and no user token payload is in the engine-change frame. We can redact any sensitive metadata and it's configurable. For Private deployments you control the control plane visibility.

[15:58] Karen Wu: Procurement question — if we need Private deployment on-prem, do you support air-gapped deployments for this workload?

[16:06] Alice Nguyen: Yes, we have an on-prem package. But note that autoscaling and burst to Hosted won't be available in a fully air-gapped setup. There's a different cost and ops model. We'll include the Private package spec.

[16:20] Jordan Lee: Can we run evals comparing int8 vs int4 on our test prompts? We need to quantify quality drop.

[16:26] Ben Carter: Absolutely. We'll run a sweep and Optimize will produce deltas per metric. We'll also export the token-level diffs if you want to do offline analysis.

[16:38] [Ben pauses, types] 

[16:45] Ben Carter: I'm starting a long run that will last ~45 minutes to capture steady-state. We'll keep the conference open and monitor. You might hear me mention log IDs — feel free to ask while we let it run. 

[16:58] Mike Patel: Quick procurement block: are there minimum commitments for Dedicated?

[17:04] Alice Nguyen: Yes, Dedicated typically has monthly or annual reserved commitments. There is a flexible burst add-on. We'll include example contracts.

[17:20] Sara Gomez: While the run continues, can we ask about observability hooks? We need tracing and correlation IDs for debugging.

[17:28] Ben Carter: We emit trace ids per request and have OpenTelemetry hooks. Console has request-level tracing and you can stream those to your SIEM. 

[17:40] Jordan Lee: What about token-level cost attribution — can we see which route or prompt template is driving cost?

[17:47] Ben Carter: Yes, Console has token cost breakdown per route and per prompt template; Optimize can recommend cheaper templates too. 

[18:00] [Background hum, intermittent typing] 

[18:20] Ben Carter: A note on the harness results so far — warm sessions show dramatically lower variance. Here are the numbers: warm P95 110ms, warm P99 240ms; cold P95 420ms, cold P99 1.2s. During the burst we observed 3% of requests routed to fallback and 1.1% transient 503s before fallback policy triggered.

[18:45] Mike Patel: That 1.1% 503 is concerning. Does it correlate with queue overflow?

[18:50] Ben Carter: Yes, those are queue-overflow rejections where router thresholds prevented escalating to fallback due to policy misconfig. We can change that to prioritize fallback over rejecting. 

[19:05] Sara Gomez: Can we set per-route cost caps to auto-disable expensive routes under extreme load?

[19:12] Ben Carter: Yes — Console supports per-route budget caps that trigger routing changes or reject new requests.

[19:30] Jordan Lee: For the follow-up POC, we want three things: 1) exact stress harness configured with our traffic; 2) a Dedicated pricing example with pinned session memory; 3) a technical deep-dive with one of your infra engineers on KV internals.

[19:50] Alice Nguyen: Noted. We'll scope that in the next email. Ben, anything else we should demo?

[19:58] Ben Carter: One last demo: controlled degradation when a model starts to hallucinate under long contexts. I have a synthetic prompt that triggers drift. 

[20:10] [Ben runs a test. AI output shows repetition] 

[20:25] Ben Carter: You can see output repeats. Optimize flagged the eval suite — auto-rollback triggered to an earlier checkpoint and we rolled a canary out. The Console shows the canary metrics and the rollback event.

[20:42] Mike Patel: Nice. How fast is an automatic rollback?

[20:47] Ben Carter: It depends on thresholds and hold windows. We did a 5-minute hold with a 3-sigma alert threshold; rollback happened within the configured 6 minutes.

[21:00] Sara Gomez: Okay team — this has been really useful. We'd like the harness and cost model. Also, we want a short write-up on best client reconnection practices.

[21:12] Alice Nguyen: We'll send those. Also we'll include a sandbox project for you to run the harness against. 

[21:22] Karen Wu: Timeline: procurement will need compliance docs and the pricing sheet — ideally by 2026-11-18.

[21:30] Alice Nguyen: We'll get them over. Ben, any closing notes?

[21:36] Ben Carter: Just that for high-burst workloads it's often a hybrid approach: Hosted for flexibility with predictive pre-warming, Dedicated for guaranteed tail SLAs where needed. Optimize and Console give you the levers to run experiments and automate rollback. 

[21:50] Mike Patel: Great. Let's schedule the POC scoping call for the week of 2026-11-22. Sara and Jordan will prepare token length histograms and concurrency targets.

[22:05] Alice Nguyen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the harness link, logs, pricing, and the draft POC scope.

[22:12] [meeting wraps; chatter; recordings finalize]

[22:30] End of recording.
